newsitem.title: USA: Daiwa expands US Treasuries' trade into cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: Daiwa expands US Treasuries' trade into cyberspace.

text.p: Daiwa Securities Co Ltd's Daiwa Securities America has expanded its trading room into cyberspace by allowing dealers to negotiate purchases and sales of U.S. government securities through the Internet, the worldwide computer network.

The first-ever government securities trade over the Internet was carried out last Friday between Daiwa and First Union Corp unit First Union Capital Markets Corp, involving $1 million in two-year Treasury notes, a Daiwa official said.
Clients will be able to log onto Daiwa Securities' network using any Internet Service Provider (ISP) and effectively close a U.S. Treasury market deal online.

Since last Friday, several other deals have already been closed, Daiwa's Gib Clark said. "Today we've already had 10 transactions," Clark, senior vice president at Daiwa Securities America Inc, told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
Clients can access Daiwa's network through the bank's new Web site -- located at http://www.oddlot.com -- and from there place their buy or sell orders.
But what about security?
Although touted as the medium of the future, security and Internet are still like water and oil.
Almost everything currently done online can be observed by third parties, unless additional instruments are incorporated into the system to ensure the user's privacy.
To skirt the security holes, Daiwa is using several mechanisms, ranging from Internet firewalls to Secure ID cards, in an effort to prevent hackers from placing rogue or phony deals into the system.
"Anybody can hook up to our Web site, but they can only get as far as our firewall. Then they have to have a Secure ID card and an account open with Daiwa," Clark said.
The so-called "secure IDs" are in fact small electronic cards that allow the user to have its entrance code to a computer network checked and changed every 60 seconds.

"The cards have an individual log-in code and a password,' Clark said. "But part of that password is changed every 60 seconds ... So even if somebody intercepts a password over the Internet, he will not be able to use it because it will be already passed," Clark added.

Clark said the system is now available only for financial institutions and brokerage houses interested in dealing with Daiwa. No individuals are allowed to open personal accounts and trade using the system at this point.
"Every new client has to pass our credit department just like any government dealer, like any institution on or off the Internet," Clark said.
The Daiwa senior vice-president said the software being used was based on an automated trading system developed by Daiwa in 1980 called The Odd-Lot Machine.
The system runs on Daiwa's own network, which currently consists of 70 institutions, most of them large primary dealers, regional dealers and big dealers banks.
Daiwa's Web site currently runs on Netscape Communications Corp software and Sun Microsystems Inc's server computers, Clark said.
Daiwa's network allows clients accessing the system via the Internet to trade any maturity in the yield curve spectrum, from one-day securities to 30-year bonds.
The minimum transaction demonination is $1,000 to a maximum of $10 million on bills, $5 million through 10-year notes and $3 million through the 30-year.
Robert Barlow of Inet Services, provider of Internet-based services to financial markets, said other instruments and markets are expected to be traded over the Internet in the coming months.
Barlow said the next introduction is likely to be foreign currency trading.
